---
title: "Risk-Based Allocation"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Risk-Based Allocation"
  description-meta: "Risk contributions, equal risk contribution portfolios and inverse volatility weighting in R, and why the package's own risk-budget objective cannot solve the problem it scores correctly."
---



Every portfolio so far has been described by how much money sits in each
position. That is not the same as how much risk sits in each position, and on
this universe the two are far apart: the minimum-variance portfolio of
@sec-09-mean-variance-theory puts most of its capital in one series and, as this
chapter measures, nearly all of its risk there too.

Allocating risk rather than capital is an old idea with a clean definition
[@qian2006; @maillard2010], a cheap approximation, and an implementation in
`PortfolioAnalytics` that does not work. We set out the decomposition that makes
the idea precise, compute the exact answer two ways, and then measure what the
package's own risk-budget objective does with a problem whose optimum it scores
correctly and cannot find.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
Re <- R - sim_riskfree_monthly$return
S  <- stats::cov(Re)
N  <- ncol(Re)
```
:::


## Allocating Risk Rather Than Capital {#sec-14-risk-based-allocation-theory}

### The decomposition that makes this precise

Portfolio volatility
$\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}) = \sqrt{\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}}$
is homogeneous of degree one in the weights, so by Euler's theorem it decomposes
exactly into additive contributions,

$$
\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{RC}_i,
\qquad
\mathrm{RC}_i = w_i \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial w_i}
= \frac{w_i\,(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w})_i}{\sigma(\boldsymbol{w})} .
$$ {#eq-14-euler}

That exactness is what makes risk budgeting possible at all, and it is the point
@qian2006 makes when he says risk budgets do add up: the shares in @eq-14-euler
are not an approximation or an attribution convention, they sum to the total by
construction. Dividing through by $\sigma$ gives shares summing to one, which is
what the code below computes.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
risk_contribution <- function(w, S) {
  marginal <- as.numeric(S %*% w)
  (w * marginal) / as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)
}

w_eq <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
round(sort(risk_contribution(w_eq, S), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 4)
#> EU_equity CH_equity UK_equity UK_credit EU_credit 
#>    0.1170    0.0973    0.0942    0.0811    0.0787
```
:::


Sixteen equally weighted series, and the largest contributes
11.7% of the risk against
6.2% of the capital. Equal capital is not equal risk,
and the gap is the entire motivation for what follows.

### Equal risk contribution

The equal risk contribution portfolio sets every term of @eq-14-euler equal,

$$
\mathrm{RC}_i = \frac{\sigma(\boldsymbol{w})}{N}
\quad \text{for every } i,
\qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad
w_i (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w})_i = w_j (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w})_j
\;\; \forall\, i, j .
$$ {#eq-14-erc}

@maillard2010 give its properties: it always exists and is unique for a long-only
portfolio, and its volatility sits between the minimum-variance portfolio's and
the equally weighted portfolio's, in that order. It has no closed form except in
special cases, but it is emphatically not a hard problem. @spinu2013 shows that
@eq-14-erc is the first-order condition of the convex program

$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{w} > 0} \;
  \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
  - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ln w_i ,
$$ {#eq-14-spinu}

whose log barrier keeps every weight strictly positive and which any convex
solver handles; @bai2016 give a least-squares formulation with the same property.
Keep @eq-14-spinu in mind for @sec-14-risk-based-allocation-application, because
the package solves this problem with a metaheuristic, and the problem is convex.

A simple fixed-point iteration converges in milliseconds.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
erc <- function(S, tol = 1e-12, max_iter = 1e5) {
  N <- ncol(S)
  w <- rep(1 / N, N)
  for (i in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    marginal <- as.numeric(S %*% w)
    w_new <- (1 / marginal) / sum(1 / marginal)   # down-weight what contributes most
    if (max(abs(w_new - w)) < tol) break
    w <- w_new
  }
  setNames(w, colnames(S))
}

w_erc <- erc(S)
c(max_deviation_from_equal = max(abs(risk_contribution(w_erc, S) - 1 / N)))
#> max_deviation_from_equal 
#>       0.0000000000003543
```
:::


Six lines, and the risk contributions are equal to machine precision. That number
is worth remembering when @sec-14-risk-based-allocation-application spends twenty
thousand function evaluations getting nowhere near it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(sort(w_erc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:6], 4)
#>    US_government        US_credit    JP_government GLOBAL_commodity 
#>           0.2210           0.0839           0.0757           0.0607 
#>    UK_government    EU_government 
#>           0.0606           0.0550
```
:::




`US_government` still receives the largest allocation, at
22.1%, because it is the least volatile series
and equalizing risk means overweighting low-volatility assets. That is a long way from the 82%
that minimum variance gives it.

### The approximation that is nearly free

@maillard2010 note a special case worth exploiting. If every pairwise correlation
equals a common $\rho$, then @eq-14-erc is solved exactly by

$$
w_i = \frac{\sigma_i^{-1}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sigma_j^{-1}},
$$ {#eq-14-inverse-vol}

inverse-volatility weighting, which needs no matrix inverse and no iteration.
Correlations here are not equal, but they are not wild either, so @eq-14-inverse-vol
should land close.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
base <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

# Exported, and rarely used. Note that it wants the portfolio object as well as
# the returns, and returns a full optimize.portfolio object rather than a vector.
w_iv <- inverse.volatility.weight(Re, base)$weights
w_iv <- w_iv[colnames(Re)]

c(l1_distance_from_erc = sum(abs(w_iv - w_erc)) / 2,
  weight_correlation   = stats::cor(w_iv, w_erc),
  max_rc_deviation     = max(abs(risk_contribution(w_iv, S) - 1 / N)))
#> l1_distance_from_erc   weight_correlation     max_rc_deviation 
#>              0.11482              0.90957              0.02699
```
:::


`inverse.volatility.weight()` is exported by `PortfolioAnalytics` and is rarely
used. It lands within 0.11 of the exact
answer in $L_1$ terms, with a weight correlation of
0.91, for the cost of one division per
asset. The approximation of @eq-14-inverse-vol is doing almost all the work that
@eq-14-erc does.

## Implementation {#sec-14-risk-based-allocation-implementation}

The package has a purpose-built objective for this. It accepts the problem,
scores it correctly, and cannot solve it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rb_spec <- base |>
  add.objective(type = "risk_budget", name = "StdDev", min_concentration = TRUE)
```
:::


### The objective is right

Before blaming a solver it is worth checking what it was asked to minimize.
`PortfolioAnalytics` exposes its own objective function, so we can score two
portfolios directly.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
score <- function(w) {
  constrained_objective(w = as.numeric(w), R = Re, portfolio = rb_spec,
                        trace = TRUE, normalize = FALSE)$out
}
c(equal_weight = score(w_eq), true_erc = score(w_erc))
#>         equal_weight             true_erc 
#> 1.150416619246363847 0.000000000000002168
```
:::


1.150 at equal weights and exactly
0.0 at the solution of @eq-14-erc. The objective is
not misspecified. It knows precisely which portfolio it wants.

### The search does not find it


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)

attempt <- function(method, ...) {
  o <- try(suppressWarnings(
    optimize.portfolio(Re, rb_spec, optimize_method = method,
                       trace = FALSE, ...)), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(o, "try-error")) {
    return(tibble::tibble(solver = method, l1_from_erc = NA_real_,
                          max_rc_dev = NA_real_, is_equal_weight = NA))
  }
  w <- extractWeights(o)[colnames(Re)]
  tibble::tibble(solver = method,
                 l1_from_erc = sum(abs(w - w_erc)) / 2,
                 max_rc_dev  = max(abs(risk_contribution(w, S) - 1 / N)),
                 is_equal_weight = isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(w), rep(1 / N, N),
                                                    tolerance = 1e-6)))
}

searches <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  attempt("DEoptim", search_size = 20000,  traceDE = 0),
  attempt("DEoptim", search_size = 200000, traceDE = 0),
  attempt("random",  search_size = 20000),
  attempt("pso"),
  attempt("GenSA")
)
#>  [1] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
#> [11] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
#>  [1] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
#> [11] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
```
:::



::: {#tbl-14-searches .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Five attempts at a problem whose answer scores zero. `is_equal_weight` asks whether the solver returned the portfolio it started from.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|              | L1 from ERC| max deviation of risk contributions|returned equal weights |
|:-------------|-----------:|-----------------------------------:|:----------------------|
|DEoptim, 20k  |      0.1931|                              0.0552|TRUE                   |
|DEoptim, 200k |      0.1931|                              0.0552|TRUE                   |
|random, 20k   |      0.1931|                              0.0552|TRUE                   |
|pso           |      0.2437|                              0.0992|FALSE                  |
|GenSA         |      0.1931|                              0.0552|TRUE                   |


:::
:::




Of the five, 4 return the equal-weighted
portfolio exactly, which is the point every one of them starts from. Ten times
the evaluation budget changes nothing. `pso` does move, and moves further from
the answer than standing still would have been.

Set beside the objective values, that is the finding: the search sits at a score
of 1.15 for two hundred thousand evaluations while a
portfolio scoring 0.0 exists and is reachable by
six lines of arithmetic.


::: {#tbl-14-comparison .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The same objective, three ways of pursuing it.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|                             | L1 from ERC| max RC deviation| volatility|
|:----------------------------|-----------:|----------------:|----------:|
|fixed point, six lines       |      0.0000|           0.0000|      6.43%|
|inverse volatility, one line |      0.1148|           0.0270|      6.96%|
|DEoptim, 20,000 evaluations  |      0.1931|           0.0552|      8.06%|


:::
:::


The one-line approximation of @eq-14-inverse-vol is closer to the answer than the
twenty-thousand-evaluation search. That is not a statement about risk parity. It
is a statement about reaching for a heuristic on a problem that
@sec-13-solvers-theory would classify as convex, given @eq-14-spinu, and which a
fixed point solves to machine precision.

### What the machinery does do

The objective is not useless. Asked for a cap rather than an equalization, it
delivers.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)
capped <- optimize.portfolio(
  Re, base |> add.objective(type = "risk_budget", name = "StdDev", max_prisk = 0.15),
  optimize_method = "DEoptim", search_size = 20000, trace = FALSE, traceDE = 0)
#>  [1] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625
#> [11] 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625 0.0625

w_cap <- extractWeights(capped)[colnames(Re)]
c(largest_risk_contribution = max(risk_contribution(w_cap, S)), cap = 0.15)
#> largest_risk_contribution                       cap 
#>                     0.117                     0.150
```
:::


A ceiling on any single risk contribution is a constraint a search can satisfy by
rejection: it has only to recognize a violation, not to locate an optimum. The
practical rule is to use the risk-budget objective for budgets and bounds, and to
compute equal risk contribution directly.

### Auditing concentration

`HHI()` and `diversification()` are exported and take a weight vector, so any
portfolio in this book can be audited for concentration in one line, including one
returned by a solver that ignored its constraint
(@sec-13-solvers-implementation).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
effective_bets <- function(w) {
  r <- risk_contribution(w, S); r <- r[r > 0]
  exp(-sum(r * log(r)))                      # the entropy of the risk shares
}

w_mv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re,
  base |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"), optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]

conc <- tibble::tibble(
  portfolio = c("equal weight", "inverse volatility", "equal risk contribution",
                "minimum variance"),
  HHI  = c(HHI(w_eq), HHI(w_iv), HHI(w_erc), HHI(w_mv)),
  div  = c(diversification(w_eq), diversification(w_iv),
           diversification(w_erc), diversification(w_mv)),
  bets = c(effective_bets(w_eq), effective_bets(w_iv),
           effective_bets(w_erc), effective_bets(w_mv)),
  vol  = c(p_vol(w_eq), p_vol(w_iv), p_vol(w_erc), p_vol(w_mv))
)
```
:::



::: {#tbl-14-concentration .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Concentration four ways. `bets` is the effective number of independent risk sources — the exponential of the entropy of the risk shares — against a maximum of sixteen.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|                        |    HHI| diversification| effective bets| volatility|
|:-----------------------|------:|---------------:|--------------:|----------:|
|equal weight            | 0.0625|          0.9375|          14.43|      8.06%|
|inverse volatility      | 0.0746|          0.9254|          15.47|      6.96%|
|equal risk contribution | 0.0922|          0.9078|          16.00|      6.43%|
|minimum variance        | 0.6815|          0.3185|           2.10|      4.13%|


:::
:::


## What Risk Parity Buys and Costs {#sec-14-risk-based-allocation-application}

### The trade, in its own units

Read the last two rows of @tbl-14-concentration together. Minimum variance
achieves 4.13% volatility with
2.1 effective bets out of sixteen. Equal
risk contribution achieves 6.43% with
exactly 16.

That is the trade in its own units: about
55 percent more
volatility for 8
times the number of independent bets. Whether it is worth taking depends on how
far the covariance matrix behind the minimum-variance answer can be trusted, and
@sec-09-mean-variance-application measured that. Resampling the same history moves
the minimum-variance portfolio by about five percent of itself, so its
concentration is at least stable.

@asness2012 give the economic argument for taking the trade anyway: if investors
are averse to leverage rather than merely to risk, they overpay for high-beta
assets, and a portfolio that equalizes risk contributions and then levers up
harvests the difference. @clarke2013 derive the analytic relationships between
risk parity, maximum diversification and minimum variance, and show that the
three coincide only under conditions this market does not satisfy.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sweep <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", window == 60,
                frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
sr_oos <- function(s) sweep$sharpe[match(s, sweep$strategy)]
to_oos <- function(s) sweep$ann_turnover[match(s, sweep$strategy)]
stopifnot(all(c("inverse_vol", "min_variance", "equal_weight", "max_sharpe")
              %in% sweep$strategy))
# The order the text states, read from the register rather than typed.
stopifnot(sr_oos("min_variance") > sr_oos("equal_weight"),
          sr_oos("equal_weight") > sr_oos("inverse_vol"),
          sr_oos("inverse_vol")  > sr_oos("max_sharpe"),
          to_oos("inverse_vol")  < to_oos("max_sharpe") / 4)
```
:::


Out of sample, inverse volatility earns a Sharpe ratio of
0.573 against minimum variance's
0.829, equal weighting's
0.626 and the tangency portfolio's
0.546 (@sec-25-backtesting-application), at
20% of
the turnover of the mean-variance optimizer, which
@sec-23-rebalancing-application converts into the Sharpe ratio each strategy
surrenders to its own trading. The risk-based portfolios are not uniformly
better: minimum variance leads all four, and inverse volatility sits between
equal weighting and the tangency portfolio before costs. They are competitive,
cheaper, and easier to explain to whoever has to sign for them.

### The covariance is a regime variable

One thing risk parity cannot escape, and it is the same thing that undermines
everything else in this book. The number of effective bets is not a property of
the portfolio. It is a property of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$
moves.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
d      <- zoo::index(Re)
in_ep  <- vapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) in_episode(d, e),
                 logical(length(d)))
calm   <- rowSums(in_ep) == 0               # outside all four episodes
crisis <- in_ep[, "credit_crisis"]

spectrum <- function(keep) {
  e <- pmax(eigen(stats::cov(zoo::coredata(Re[keep, ])), symmetric = TRUE,
                  only.values = TRUE)$values, 0)
  c(months = sum(keep), pc1_share = e[1] / sum(e), directions = sum(e)^2 / sum(e^2))
}
regime <- rbind(calm = spectrum(calm), crisis = spectrum(crisis))
stopifnot(regime["crisis", "pc1_share"] > regime["calm", "pc1_share"],
          regime["crisis", "directions"] < regime["calm", "directions"] / 2)
round(regime, 3)
#>        months pc1_share directions
#> calm      320     0.369      4.800
#> crisis      7     0.760      1.664
```
:::


@sec-07-covariance-matrix-application measured it on these sixteen series, and
the measurement repeats here: outside the four episodes of `sim_episodes` the
first principal component carries
37% of the variance and the
matrix behaves like 4.8
independent directions; through the credit crisis it carries
76% and the count falls
to 1.7, a figure that the
short window exaggerates and that calm windows of the same length still do not
reach. A portfolio constructed to hold sixteen equal risk contributions in calm
months holds about 2
independent bets when it matters.

Risk parity does not solve that. It measures risk more honestly than capital
weighting does, and then allocates against an estimate that halves precisely when
the allocation is tested. @roncalli2013 treats the estimation problem at length,
and @sec-19-regimes-theory is where this book confronts it rather than noting
it.

### Budgets that are not equal

Equal risk contribution is the special case of a more general idea. A risk budget
assigns each asset a share $b_i$ with $\sum_i b_i = 1$ and asks for weights
satisfying

$$
\mathrm{RC}_i = b_i \,\sigma(\boldsymbol{w})
\quad \text{for every } i ,
$$ {#eq-14-budget}

which reduces to @eq-14-erc when $b_i = 1/N$. @roncalli2013 develops the general
case, and the convex program of @eq-14-spinu generalizes directly by replacing
the uniform coefficient on the log barrier with $b_i$. The fixed point in this
chapter generalizes just as easily, dividing the marginal contributions by the
budget before renormalizing.

The interest of @eq-14-budget is that it is the natural language of a mandate. A
policy statement rarely says hold twenty percent in credit; it says credit may
consume no more than a quarter of the risk. Those are different instructions and
only the second survives a change in volatility. This is also the form in which
the package's own objective is usable, as the `max_prisk` result above showed:
bounds on @eq-14-budget are checkable by rejection, and a search can satisfy them.

### Hierarchical risk parity

The methods in this chapter all require $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and most require
its inverse, which @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory showed is where the estimate
is weakest. @lopezdeprado2016 proposes an alternative that avoids inversion
entirely. Hierarchical risk parity clusters the assets on a distance derived from
their correlations, orders them so that similar assets are adjacent, and then
allocates by recursive bisection: split the ordered set in two, allocate between
the halves in inverse proportion to their variances, and recurse.

Nothing in that procedure inverts a matrix, so it is defined even when
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is singular, which by @eq-07-rank is the normal case at
instrument level. The claim is that the resulting portfolios are more stable out
of sample than either minimum variance or equal risk contribution, because the
quantity being estimated, a clustering, is far coarser than a full inverse.

The method belongs with the sleeve structure of
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory rather than here, because what it is
really doing is imposing a hierarchy on the universe and allocating down it. It
is mentioned here because it is the obvious next question once risk
contributions are on the table, and because it is the one widely used technique
in this area that `PortfolioAnalytics` does not implement at all.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- Portfolio volatility decomposes exactly into additive risk contributions by
  @eq-14-euler. The shares are not an attribution convention; they sum to the
  total by construction [@qian2006].
- Equal capital is not equal risk. Sixteen equally weighted series here put
  12% of the risk in
  one of them, against 6.2% of the capital.
- The equal risk contribution portfolio of @eq-14-erc always exists, is unique
  long-only, and sits between minimum variance and equal weighting in volatility
  [@maillard2010].
- It is not a hard problem. @eq-14-spinu is a convex program with a log barrier,
  and a six-line fixed point reaches machine precision. The package nonetheless
  routes it to a metaheuristic.
- Of five solvers, 4 hand back the equally
  weighted portfolio they started from, and a tenfold budget changes nothing. The one-line inverse-volatility
  approximation of @eq-14-inverse-vol is closer to the answer than a
  twenty-thousand-evaluation search.
- Use the risk-budget objective for caps and budgets, which a search can satisfy
  by rejection, and compute equal risk contribution directly.
- Risk parity buys about
  8 times the
  effective bets for about
  55 percent more
  volatility, and out of sample inverse volatility lands between equal weighting
  and the tangency portfolio at a fraction of the latter's turnover.
- The effective number of bets is a property of the covariance matrix, not of the
  portfolio, and it falls by more than half going into the credit crisis.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Run the fixed-point `erc()` on a covariance matrix estimated from the months
   outside the four episodes of `sim_episodes` only, then apply the resulting
   weights to the months of the credit crisis. How equal are the realized risk
   contributions?
2. `inverse.volatility.weight()` ignores correlations entirely. Construct a
   universe where that is catastrophic — two nearly identical series and one
   independent one — and report the risk contributions it produces.
3. Repeat @tbl-14-searches with a `max_prisk` objective instead of
   `min_concentration`. Do the solvers agree with each other? Does the budget
   bind?
4. The effective-bets measure uses entropy. Replace it with `1 / sum(rc^2)`, the
   inverse Herfindahl of the risk shares, and recompute @tbl-14-concentration.
   Which portfolios change rank, and which measure would you defend to a client?
